title: Quick guide for incident scenarios
markdown:
Use **Lucene** mode in the developer log dashboard. Choose the incident window, start with 15–30 minutes and keep Live updates off while investigating a fixed incident. Replace example IDs and deployment names with your own.

## 1. Find HTTP logs by status code

All recorded HTTP statuses (100–599; excludes non-HTTP/default status 0):

```lucene
http_status:[100 TO 599]
```

One status code:

```lucene
http_status:500
```

| Query | Includes |
| --- | --- |
| `http_status>100` | 100–199 |
| `http_status>200` | 200–299 |
| `http_status>300` | 300–399 |
| `http_status>400` | 400–499 |
| `http_status>500` | 500–599 |

This custom shorthand includes its starting code. `http_status>403` means 403–499. It requires no spaces and applies only in Lucene. `http_status:>500` and SQL `http_status > 500` remain strictly greater than 500. On older images use `http_status:[500 TO 599]` for 5xx.

## 2. Find logs for a Google trace

Copy the trace ID from the GCP log or trace details, then search across deployments:

```lucene
trace_id:"EXAMPLE_TRACE_ID"
```

A Google log can contain either an ID or a resource name such as `projects/PROJECT_ID/traces/EXAMPLE_TRACE_ID`. If our `trace_id` stores just the ID, use the part after `/traces/`. If it stores the full name, search that full value instead. Expand a known matching log to confirm the stored format; this guide does not assume the ingestion pipeline converts it. [Google trace field reference](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/reference/v2/rest/v2/LogEntry#FIELDS.trace).

Keep the trace search free of deployment filters initially so you can follow the request across services. Add `trace_id` to the summary. Missing trace IDs cannot be found through that column; verify whether the ID exists elsewhere in the expanded payload.

## 3. Find a keyword or phrase

A keyword within one deployment:

```lucene
deployment_name:"affiliate-portal-api" AND timeout
```

A phrase or path fragment with punctuation:

```lucene
deployment_name:"affiliate-portal-api" AND "split-commission/v2"
```

Either keyword, excluding a noisy phrase:

```lucene
deployment_name:"affiliate-portal-api" AND (timeout OR refused) AND NOT "health check"
```

Prefer a known deployment and incident window before broad free-text or wildcard searches. Quotes keep a phrase together; they do not guarantee an indexed lookup or instant seven-day results.

## 4. Find an HTTP method and URL

POST requests to the transactions path, including URLs with query parameters:

```lucene
http_request_method:"POST" AND http_request_url:*/payments/transactions/*
```

Only 5xx failures on that route, using syntax supported before custom.70 too:

```lucene
http_request_method:"POST" AND http_request_url:*/payments/transactions/* AND http_status:[500 TO 599]
```

For an exact URL, quote the complete value copied from the log:

```lucene
http_request_method:"GET" AND http_request_url:"https://api.example.com/payments/transactions/"
```

Replace the example host. Exact matching includes the query string if present. Use the wildcard path query when host names or query parameters vary. These columns only match logs where HTTP fields are populated.

## 5. Find slow HTTP requests

`http_latency_seconds` records HTTP request duration in **seconds**; it is not the time HyperDX takes to run a search.

| Query | Finds requests taking |
| --- | --- |
| `http_latency_seconds:>0.5` | More than 500 ms |
| `http_latency_seconds:>1` | More than 1 second |
| `http_latency_seconds:>5` | More than 5 seconds |

Requests taking more than 1 second:

```lucene
http_latency_seconds:>1
```

Slow POST requests to the transactions route:

```lucene
http_request_method:"POST" AND http_request_url:*/payments/transactions/* AND http_latency_seconds:>2
```

Use a colon before the comparison operator. These are strict comparisons: `:>1` excludes exactly 1 second. Only logs with populated latency values can identify slow requests; a missing/default zero does not prove the request was fast.
